Title: Significance of Westernizing, Democratising, and Secularizing the Turkish Education System

Background: From Ottoman modernization projects to the Kemalist Republic
- Ottoman reformers pursued Tanzimat-era modernization by importing European pedagogical ideas, legal frameworks, and institutional models to strengthen state capacity and technical know-how, with figures trained in France introducing Western epistemologies and curricula that challenged medrese-centered learning and promoted nationalism, freedom, and modern instructional methods in Turkish schools by the late 19th century <cite id="749db311-0">During the Tanzimat era many Turkish educators were inspired by French epistemology, and asserted that the Medrese mentality needed to be abandoned in order to build a modern society</cite> <cite id="749db311-1">The Westernization of Turkey aimed to make political changes in the individual life and social institutions in a democratic direction, improve industrialization for the economy and use science as a reference for higher order of thinking</cite>. 
- Foreign educational missions and experts (French, German, Austrian, American) played an instrumental role: reports, teaching posts, and consultancy flooded into military academies, medical schools, and universities, with notable waves after 1730s (French/German), 19th-century Austrian medical instructors, and a large German faculty at Istanbul University post–World War I; French language and institutions (e.g., Galatasaray Lycée) became privileged pillars of elite formation and modeled curricula <cite id="749db311-2">Educators and experts brought in from the West due to various topics have become another dynamic force that influenced Westernization in Turkish education system</cite> <cite id="749db311-3">John Dewey and Albert Malche were among two educators involved in the Westernization movement who came to study and write reports on the Turkish Higher Educational System</cite> <cite id="749db311-4">French influence dominated the cultural field from the 18th century onward, with French becoming the privileged language of higher education by the 19th century</cite> <cite id="749db311-2">During World War I, about 19 faculty members under the chairmanship of Franz Schmidt came to Turkey to teach at Istanbul University (Darülfünun)</cite>.

Westernizing significance: technology transfer, cosmopolitan capital, and elite formation
- By adopting European curricula, languages, and institutional templates, Turkey’s education system internalized scientific-rationalist epistemologies and managerial/technical competencies that underpinned state-building and industrialization aims; French schooling trained elites in modern culture and governance models, while missionary schools and capitulations facilitated “Westernization” but also ethnic segregation, signaling both integration into global modernity and layered inequalities <cite id="749db311-1">The Westernization of Turkey aimed to make political changes in the individual life and social institutions in a democratic direction, improve industrialization for the economy and use science as a reference for higher order of thinking</cite> <cite id="749db311-4">French influence dominated the cultural field from the 18th century onward (Ergün 1990), with French becoming the privileged language of higher education by the 19th century</cite>. 
- Direct incorporation of Western expertise in teaching and administration catalyzed pedagogical change: German and Austrian instructors embedded modern medical and military education, while French and international experts shaped higher education structures and policies; this transnationalism channeled “scientific solutions” to societal problems and framed modernity as a scientific, secular, and rights-based project <cite id="749db311-2">Educators and experts brought in from the West ... taught almost in all of the institutions in higher education including military schools of Turkey</cite> <cite id="749db311-3">In terms of Westernization efforts in Turkish education system, obtaining reports from foreign experts and educators continued a fashion of continuous trend even during the Republican era</cite>. 
- Symbolic-structural shifts (Latin alphabet, metric system, adoption of Gregorian calendar, Westernized civic aims) signaled alignment with Europe and cultivated “thinking and behaving like Europeans,” embedding Western cultural norms and civic scripts into education as a civilizing mission; these instruments also had immediate functional payoffs in literacy and administrative coordination <cite id="ebccee77-2">The Latin based alphabet was mandated by law on 1 November 1928, significantly increasing literacy within a short time frame</cite> <cite id="ebccee77-3">Ataturk tried to make the Turkish people able to think, behave, and even dress like Europeans</cite> <cite id="ebccee77-2">The most significant reform ... came in 1933 ... abolished the Istanbul Darulfunun ... and turned into a university</cite>.

Secularizing significance: state-society remaking and ideological hegemony
- Kemalist reforms used education as a vehicle for radical secularization: abolition of the caliphate (1924), the Tevhid-i Tedrisat Law (1924) centralized and unified the system under the Ministry of National Education, closed religious schools, and severed Islamic bodies’ supervision, replacing divinity-centered syllabi with rational-scientific methods; the 1933 University Reform dismantled Darülfünun’s juristic-medrese logic and recast Istanbul into a secular university framework <cite id="ebccee77-1">The establishment of modern Turkey has led the implementation of reformation and modernization processes ... Mustafa Kemal Atatürk ... focused on the secularization process to modernize both the state and the Turkish society</cite> <cite id="ebccee77-1">Atatürk's secular approach was radical and assertive ... separating public affairs from religion as a whole</cite> <cite id="ebccee77-1">The unification of education system made religious education to be marginalized and no longer functioning and caused its elimination under the new law</cite> <cite id="ebccee77-2">On the same day, another revolutionary law aiming at unification, standardization, and secularization of the educational institutions (Tevhid-i Tedrisat kanunu) was passed. This law closed the religious schools and attached all educational institutions to the Ministry of National Education</cite> <cite id="ebccee77-2">The Latin based alphabet was mandated by law on 1 November 1928, significantly increasing literacy within a short time frame</cite> <cite id="ebccee77-4">The closing of Darülfünun in 1933 and the subsequent establishment of Istanbul University represented a significant turning point ... substituting a university structure that valued secular sciences over theology</cite>. 
- The Kemalist project redefined state-society relations by erasing multicultural Ottoman legacies and retooling education as a site of secular citizenship and scientific rationality: transnational scholars and institutions (e.g., French lycées) were enlisted in producing “legitimate knowledge” and cultivating a skilled, secular workforce, with French language and pedagogy acting as instruments of ideological and administrative transformation <cite id="749db311-4">French dominance was challenged with increasing German influence ... French institutions like the (still active) Lycée de Galatasaray trained elites in French culture and served as educational models</cite> <cite id="749db311-4">Education stood out as a central pillar of Turkey's reconstruction ... producing and disseminating legitimate knowledge, redefining state-society relations distinct from the Ottoman multicultural legacy, cultivating national identity and a skilled workforce</cite>. 
- The pedagogical purge of divinity and the elevation of science framed secularization as civilizational progress; however, Atatürk’s radical stance also sought to eradicate Islam’s hegemonic role in Turkish identity, embedding a hegemonic secular ideology that marginalized religious education and produced a unilingual, secular public culture <cite id="ebccee77-1">This attempt portrays Kemalist vision to eradicate the role of Islam that has shaped the identity of the Turkish nation for a long time</cite> <cite id="ebccee77-1">At the same time, the educational syllabus was framed by undermining divinity elements and applying only on rational and scientific-based methodologies</cite>.

Democratizing significance: mass literacy, inclusion, and expanded access
- Education became a core instrument of mass modernization: the Latin alphabet (1928) was explicitly tied to literacy campaigns, and by 1933 the state had standardized curricula and institutions nationwide; the 1933 higher-education law expanded access to science-based universities while dismantling exclusive juristic tracks, diffusing modern knowledge and credentials across society <cite id="ebccee77-2">The Latin based alphabet was mandated by law on 1 November 1928, significantly increasing literacy within a short time frame</cite> <cite id="ebccee77-2">The most significant reform ... abolished the Istanbul Darulfunun ... turning into a university</cite>. 
- Gender and social mobility were transformed by rapid policy sequencing: the Republic prioritized fast, politically backed reforms; female literacy rose from 10% (1935) to 94% (2015), evidencing broad democratizing gains; yet gender gaps persisted (1.8% illiteracy among men vs. 9.0% among women aged 25+ in 2015), underscoring structural inequalities that reforms sought to overcome <cite id="34e9f172-1">Whereas the rate of female literacy in Turkey was 10% in 1935 ... 55% in 1980 ... 81% in 2000 and 94% in 2015</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-1">However, women still constitute a significant part of illiterate population ... 9.0% of women 25 years of age or older are illiterate, this rate is 1.8% for men</cite>. 
- Democratization of higher education unfolded in two waves: mass expansion from 76 universities (53 public) in 1981 to 208 by 2021–22, including 41 new public universities launched in 2006–07 to reach rural communities; this proliferative policy extended access to regions long excluded, though quality and autonomy concerns mounted alongside politicization <cite id="34e9f172-2">Thanks to the previous legal framework put into action in 1981 ... the momentous increase in number of universities occurred in 1992 when 21 new universities were integrated ... in 2006 and 2007, government established 41 public universities mostly in less developed cities</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-4">Before the aKP came to power in November 2002, there existed seventy-six universities ... The data of 2021-2022 ... show that there were 208 universities, seventy-five of which were private non-profit</cite>. 
- Constitutional guarantees extended inclusion: the 1982 Constitution enshrined free basic education (grades 1–12) and state control over curricula, while the 1981 law institutionalized a unified system from preschool to higher education; refugee children’s schooling has been a test of these commitments, with 63.3% enrolled by 2020 and legal pathways for Syrian students to access Turkish universities under the 2014 Foreigners and International Protection Law <cite id="34e9f172-3">All children including those of foreign nationality have the right to a free "basic education" in public schools up to grade 12</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-3">Under the auspices of the National Education Basic Law No. 1739, the Ministry of Education controls basic education ... private schools are fee-paying institutions</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-3">By January, 2020, 63.3% of the 1,820,172 school-age children from refugee backgrounds received an education in Turkey ... 98.4% ... registered in legal education institutions operated by the Ministry of National Education</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-3">In 2014, the government passed the "Law on Foreigners and International Protection" ... identifying the function and implementation of protection policies including free education</cite>. 
- Politically, the 1995 legalization of opposition parties democratized contestation within a civil framework, enabling plural universities to contribute to public discourse; scholars stress that democratizing reforms must be protected from autocratic backsliding because university autonomy is pivotal for innovation and academic freedom <cite id="34e9f172-4">Following its rise to power in November 2002, the aKP implemented a policy of proliferating higher education institutions ... as the extension of political power</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-0">Autonomy of academia and academic freedoms remained standstill and even seriously fell back ... political campaign, titled "a university for each province" ... advocated inevitable increase in the number of universities</cite>. 

Trade-offs, conflicts, and reversals: inclusion vs. ethnic/religious stratification; laiklik vs. resurgence of religion
- Westernizing instruments brought both integration and stratification: missionary schools, capitulations, and language hierarchies reinforced “Westernization” while entrenching ethnic/religious segregation alongside broader modernization, revealing a dual legacy of cosmopolitan learning and unequal cultural power relations <cite id="749db311-4">Foreign and minority schools reinforced "Westernisation" but also ethnic segregation of the empire</cite>. 
- Secularizing reforms faced enduring social costs: marginalizing Islamic education and identity knowledge provoked resistance; phases of policy oscillated between strict marginalization (1924–48) and pragmatic accommodations (late 1930s–1948) as the state tried to reconcile secular goals with cultural realities and demands for religious education <cite id="ebccee77-1">Atatürk's secular approach was radical and assertive ... marginalizing political affairs from religion but also tended to separate public affairs from religion as a whole</cite> <cite id="ebccee77-4">These phases reflect ... 1924-1930 ... secularize education and establish state control ... 1930-1939 ... heightened secularization ... 1940-1948 ... pragmatic response to public demand for religious education</cite>. 
- Democratization gains have been contested and uneven: massification and inclusive schooling were leveraged for social mobility, but politicization under the AKP era expanded religious organizations (e.g., Diyanet-linked student bodies) in provincial universities, reframing them as political extensions rather than purely academic spaces; autonomy and academic freedom have repeatedly come under pressure, with rectors appointed through centralized presidential power and universities mobilized as instruments of cultural hegemony <cite id="34e9f172-4">Most of these universities served as an important tool for the aKP aim to establish cultural hegemony and nurture a "pious generation" as opposed to the "infidel generation" republican Turkey had educated</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-4">YÖK became responsible for nominating three candidates ... the President ... appointed one of these three candidates</cite>. 
- Gender democratization advanced dramatically but remains incomplete: literacy surged, yet women aged 25+ still had higher illiteracy than men, and curricular shifts (e.g., 4+4+4 system from 2012) altered participation patterns for girls, indicating persistent socioeconomic and policy-related tensions even within formal inclusion <cite id="34e9f172-1">Women still constitute a significant part of illiterate population ... 9.0% of women ... are illiterate, this rate is 1.8% for men</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-2">Turkey ... regulated the compulsory education period ... as 12 years; however, this system ... adversely affected participation of the girls in the education process</cite>. 
- Transnational modernization and national construction remain intertwined: scholarship emphasizes that Turkey’s education system has been shaped by “Westernisation” as a unidirectional import of European expertise and models, yet post-2016 shifts (mass dismissals, politicized appointments) have eroded autonomy and raised concerns about the long-run capacity of universities to serve as engines of innovation and civic dialogue <cite id="749db311-4">Turkey has been a unidirectional importer of European expertise, which shaped its educational field through competing models, expertise, and languages</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-0">There occurred five mass exportations ... in 1933, 1947, 1960, 1971 and 1983 in Turkish Universities ... rectorate elections are always referred to as political decisions ... Autonomy of academia and academic freedoms remained standstill and even seriously fell back</cite>.

Synthesis: why these reforms mattered
- Westernizing, secularizing, and democratizing the education system collectively remade Turkey as a nation-state: they transferred scientific and managerial knowledge, installed a secular legal-civic order, and expanded schooling to produce a literate, meritocratic citizenry capable of industrialization and participation in democratic politics <cite id="749db311-1">Westernization refers to the establishment of a system based on science and technology in the life of a society where the principles of freedom and equality are adopted as the basis of human rights</cite> <cite id="ebccee77-1">Atatürk's secular approach ... tended to separate public affairs from religion as a whole</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-1">The rate of female literacy in Turkey was 10% in 1935 ... 94% in 2015</cite>. 
- The significance is multi-dimensional: culturally, alignment with Europe forged new civic scripts and identities; economically, scientific curricula and mass education underpinned industrialization and administrative capacity; politically, democratizing access and contested pluralism enabled modern governance while exposing enduring tensions between laiklik and popular religiosity; and socially, education catalyzed gendered mobility and inclusion, even as regional and gender gaps persisted <cite id="ebccee77-3">Ataturk tried to make the Turkish people able to think, behave, and even dress like Europeans</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-2">Government established 41 public universities mostly in less developed cities as a part of regional development policy</cite> <cite id="34e9f172-1">Women still constitute a significant part of illiterate population ... 9.0% of women ... are illiterate, this rate is 1.8% for men</cite>. 
- The ongoing significance today lies in the interplay of inclusion and control: education remains the key site where Westernizing knowledge, secular law, and democratizing access meet popular religious sensibilities and political centralization; sustaining democratic gains requires defending academic autonomy and anti-discriminatory schooling, as mass expansion must be coupled with quality assurance and cultural integration to avoid politicization and regressions of civic equality <cite id="34e9f172-0">Autonomy of academia and academic freedoms remained standstill and even seriously fell back ... political campaign, titled "a university for each province"</cite> <cite id="749db311-4">Foreign and minority schools reinforced "Westernisation" but also ethnic segregation of the empire</cite>.

Limitations and open questions
- Quantifying causal attribution for macro outcomes (e.g., growth, democracy metrics) requires disentangling education reforms from broader structural changes; nonetheless, literacy trajectories and systemic expansion provide strong evidence of democratizing and modernizing impact <cite id="34e9f172-1">Whereas the rate of female literacy in Turkey was 10% in 193510% in , 19% in 195010% in , 55% in 198010% in , 81% in 200010% in and 94% in 201510% in</cite>. 
- Future work should triangulate administrative, curricular, and survey data to assess how secularized curricula and Westernized languages shaped agency, identity, and inter-ethnic relations over generations, and to evaluate policy reversals’ effects on innovation, equity, and democratic legitimacy in higher education <cite id="34e9f172-4">University autonomy could not remain unaffected ... the bill ... entrusted the authority of appointing university rectors directly to the President</cite>.

In particular, the Westernization of Turkey rests on three crucial historical turns: firstly, a series of continuous military defeats caused Turks to aggressively modernization as a way to militarily and technologically compete with other Western nations; secondly, the early designers of Turkish secular state relied heavily on French understandings and approaches. Westernization refers to the establishment of a system based on science and technology in the life of a society where the principles of freedom and equality are adopted as the basis of human rights. This process also provides scientific solutions for the problems encountered in both individual and social life (Ergün, 1990). Westernization basically encourages developing countries to learn and then use what the West has found in science, technology, human rights, prosperity, and art (Başgöz, 2005). This section demonstrates how Turkey's Westernization efforts, which then have effected its education system. 

The first efforts of Westernization in Turkey started during Ottoman State at the end of 18th century (Karpat, Durukan, & Durukan 2002). At that time, Europe still was not at a stage of widely using the scientific applications for steam or mines. However, by the 19th century, Europe had substantial advancements in several areas including education. Such improvements made Turkish authorities believe that Europe was modern and that Turkey needed to do what was possible to reach to the same level of technology and education (Çetinkaya, 2002). The Westernization of Turkey aimed to make political changes in the individual life and social institutions in a democratic direction, improve industrialization for the economy and use science as a reference for higher order of thinking (Koçer, 1983). In efforts of creating a modern Turkish society, many Turkish political and educational elites had their trainings specifically from France during the Ottomans era. The French culture and language were considered as one of the modern languages of the time (Mignolo, 2009). The French culture and the use of their language effected Turkish state and its educational leaders about where to go in terms of obtaining their educational training during that time.

Educators and experts brought in from the West due to various topics have become another dynamic force that influenced Westernization in Turkish education system. They taught almost in all of the institutions in higher education including military schools of Turkey (Kaplan, 1999). They were first brought from France, and then educators from other European countries and the United States joined them. Some of them worked as teachers, some only provided reports on educational praxis (Turan, 2000). Turkish education system was easily adapted to Western teaching methodologies as there a heavy presence of the experts and educators from the West in Turkish schools during that time. 

The oldest report provided to Ottomans by French experts in terms of Westernization was the one provided by French officer named De Rocheford. He wrote reports about the establishment of a foreign army unit in the Ottoman army in 1716. In 1732, some reports about printing press were also provided by French experts (Zürcher & Gönen, 1999). Claude Alexandre Comte de Bonneval, who actually served in Ottoman army, brought in more French officers to serve after 1730s. In addition, after 1781, Baron de Tott, who came to Istanbul with French ambassador, did substantial work in naval academy. In 1798, at the request of Selim III, German officers joined the army's modernization with the arrival of Officer Von Goetze. In 19th century, Kari Ambrosso Bernard and Sigmund Spitzer, who were from Austria, were the instructors in Turkish medical schools. During the World War I, about 19 faculty members under the chairmanship of Franz Schmidt came to Turkey to teach at Istanbul University (Darülfünun) (Koçer, 1983). 

In terms of Westernization efforts in Turkish education system, obtaining reports from foreign experts and educators continued a fashion of continuous trend even during the Republican era (After 1923) (Kaplan, 1999). Title: Mobilising Transnational Expertise in National Construction: Exiled Academics and the Transformation of Interwar Turkey
Snippet: Among the many sectors transformed by transnational expertise, education stood out as a central pillar of Turkey's reconstruction. This sector warrants attention not only for its extensive integration of transnational expertise but also for its role as a driving force behind national construction serving both ideological and practical purposes: producing and disseminating legitimate knowledge, redefining state-society relations distinct from the Ottoman multicultural legacy, cultivating national identity and a skilled workforce. 

In this context, the role of transnational scholars in Ottoman and Republican education has garnered considerable scholarly attention, with recent studies, like Sarmis (2019) on the "transnational construction of the Turkish education system", highlighting continuities between the two eras. Existing scholarship often interprets this transnationalism through the lens of "Westernisation", reflecting asymmetries in circulations and exchanges. Since the late Ottoman period, Turkey has been a unidirectional importer of European expertise, which shaped its educational field through competing models, expertise, and languages. 

French influence dominated the cultural field from the 18th century onward (Ergün 1990), with French becoming the privileged language of higher education by the 19th century (Ergin 1977). French institutions like the (still active) Lycée de Galatasaray (a joint Ottoman-French project established in 1868) trained elites in French culture and served as educational models (Georgeon 1994;Gürtunca 2017). French dominance was challenged with increasing German influence, as seen in schools like the Alman Lisesi (1868-), which became bastions of German culture (Kılıç 2005;Ortaylı 1981;Widmann 2000). By the end of the century, American colleges such as Roberts College, alongside British, Italian, Russian, and Greek schools, also proliferated. As part of missionary activities, supported by capitulations granting extra-territorial rights and privileges to Western powers, foreign and minority schools reinforced "Westernisation" but also ethnic segregation of the empire (Göçek 1993;Kılıç 2005;Sezer 1999). 

Concurrently, Ottoman reformers invested in education as a lever for social change and survival in a threatening geopolitical environment.

Title: Questioning Administration Processes and Autonomy of Higher Education System in Turkey
Snippet: Higher education policies have always been on the agenda of decision makers and politicians in Turkey. Almost every government has changed some certain bodies and structural organizations as well as employment policies at higher education institutions in Turkey. Regarding all changes in the university bodies, it is possible to claim that the history of Turkish universities is also a history of vicious educational reforms as well as "history of exportations". Until 2016, for example, there occurred five mass exportations or dismisses in 1933, 1947, 1960, 1971 and 1983 in Turkish Universities (Mazıcı, 1995). Just before further mass exportations in 2016 and 2017 Turkish government has noted many unusual and radical changes since the early 2000s. For instance, rectorate elections are always referred to as political decisions by ruling governments and presidents and cause many allegations among public and mass media. The election system was partially representation of faculty members before the government removed system of presidency elections held for universities in November, 2016 by means of a decree law no.676 after military coup attempt in July, 2016. Despite the fact that it was a questionable step in terms of representation of faculty members and autonomy of academia, none of the university senates could publish a message questioning the decision. Even before the military coup attempt in July, 2016, the government took several controversial decisions for universities. Autonomy of academia and academic freedoms remained standstill and even seriously fell back. It went seriously worse just after academics for peace petition and signature campaign in January 2016. Many of the signatory academics were criticized harshly by the government and exported from their positions through decree laws just after the military coup attempt in July 2016. On the other hand political campaign, titled "a university for each province" and started in 2006-2007, has advocated inevitable increase in the number of universities and rising demand for many academic personnel to run education processes at the university bodies. The campaign resulted in building up many new universities even in far rural areas of Turkey. Question of quality of education, employment policies, infrastructure and over-education have emerged as more serious educational, social, cultural and financial problems. This paper discusses changes in higher education policies in Turkey from the late Ottoman rule to recent processes. The current study is a descriptive analysis of qualitative and quantitative data based on literature review and text analysis of the newspaper articles and statistical analysis of the data released by Council of Higher Education.

Title: Economics of Higher Education and Contemporary Outlook of Turkish Universities
Snippet: Thanks to the previous legal framework put into action in 1981, five different institutions were running in Turkish higher education comprising universities, academies, 2-year vocational schools and conservatories, 3-year education institutions belonging to Ministry of Education and distance learning named as YAYKUR (Do¤ramac›, 2007). In the meantime, vocational schools, conservatories and 3-year educational institutions were connected to university administrations with couple of official amendments. The momentous increase in number of universities occurred in 1992 when 21 new universities were integrated into the sector. Furthermore, in 2006 and 2007, government established 41 public universities mostly in less developed cities as a part of regional development policy. The chief motivation behind university founding can be articulated as "the governmental aspiration for provision of mass education" (Onder and Onder, 2011). 

YÖK is the main administrative body to manage universities in Turkey. With variations among public and non-profit universities, the university administrators -deans and rectors in particular-are appointed within the YÖK's regulative procedures. However, the heads of board of directors in non-profit universities seize more managerial power than appointed rectors. The other supervisory organization in Turkish higher education is Interuniversity Council of Turkey (Üniversiteler Aras› Kurul, ÜAK) which has a responsibility to coordinate universities in terms of academic well-being as well as organize the associate professorship exam. The candidates must fulfill certain requirements such as publishing papers in SSCI journals at least one in national journal. 

The aforementioned supervisory entities bear the crucial question in minds is that to what extent Turkish universities are autonomous in decision-making process. Due to the fact that autonomy is the driving force behind innovation and keeping pace with cutting-edge academic enhancement, universities should have more autonomous administrative bodies than any other institution. Current OECD statistics about the level of autonomy in universities do not have optimistic signs for Turkey. Whereas Turkey's score is nearly 1.5 which is one of the lowest, Denmark had 6, Norway 5, Austria 4.5 and South Korea 2.5. These scores stipulate less influence from supervisory institutions (YÖK and ÜAK) as well as more emphasis on university-based decision-making.

On the subject of the increasing refugee population, education policies and services for foreigners are now garnering much more interest in Turkey (Icduygu ve Simsek, 2016;Coskun and Emin, 2016), given the longevity of the crisis in Syria. 

By January, 2020, 63.3% of the 1,820,172 school-age children from refugee backgrounds received an education in Turkey. 98.4% (648,108) of refugee children who go to school are registered in legal education institutions operated by the Ministry of National Education. Given that education is a significant contributor to saving Syrian children from becoming another 'lost generation', for this reason Turkish national education policies and procedures are being developed by educators, government bureaucrats and civil society organizations to meet the learning needs of refugee students (Dallal, 2016). The Turkish Ministry of Education released an outline in 2013 that highlighted its responsibility to provide learning opportunities for Syrian refugee children. On this basis the responsibility to arrange the curriculum for Syrian students is that of the Ministry of Education of the Syrian Interim Government. The plan also states that Syrians who graduated from high school and passed the exams enabling them to enroll in university in Syria can now register in Turkish universities. In 2014, the government passed the "Law on Foreigners and International Protection" relying on the outline announced in 2013. As a legal framework, the law identified the function and implementation of protection policies including free education, healthcare, and social assistance for refugees in Turkey (Ineli-Ciger, 2016).

Title: Westernization of 'Darülfünun' and its Impacts on Religious Education in Turkish Universities
Snippet: He was sent to Europe to research the educational systems there and compile a report on Italy's experience and vocational schooling (Ergün, 1990). 

More Turkish educators with knowledge of European educational systems offered more reports to suggest a contemporary Turkish educational system. Necmettin Arif, Kemal Zaim, and Tunal Hilmi Bey provide a report on the French educational system for this reason, while Turkish scholars like Mehmed Sabahattin, Nafi Atuf Kansu, and Abdullah Cevdet Bey declared that the British and American educational systems are superior to the French ones (Akyüz, 2001). They therefore want to have an impact on the new British and American-based Turkish educational system. Others in the Turkish academic community contend that the German educational system is superior to that of other Western nations (Kaplan, 2019). As can be seen, many experts wanted to have an impact on the creation of the contemporary Türkiye's educational system after being impressed by the educational philosophy and system in Europe (Adanalı, 2004). 

Furthermore, during the Tanzimat era many Turkish educators were inspired by French epistemology, and asserted that the Medrese mentality needed to be abandoned in order to build a modern society. These educators included Ziya Pasha, Namık Kemal, and Ali Suavi (Akyüz, 2001). Ziya Pasha translated Jean Jacques Rousseau's pedagogical work "Emile" into Turkish for a similar reason. The concepts of nationalism and freedom were introduced into Turkish education by Namık Kemal. Selim Sabit Efendi, who studied in Paris between 1855 and 1861, wrote the first educational book in the Ottoman State that was based on the Western educational system (Zürcher, 2004). Their works had a significant influence at the time on the introduction of fresh instructional strategies, resources, and tools in Turkish schools. 

During the second constitutional period (II. Meşrutiyet), significant discussions on the adaptation and dissemination of Western pedagogical ideas took place in Türkiye's educational thought between 1908 and 1920. Emrullah Efendi was a significant educator and stakeholder in the period. Emrullah Efendi offered some advice for the revamped Turkish educational system.

Title: The Effects of Westernization Efforts on the Turkish Education System
Snippet: The new education system in Turkey was shaped through the efforts made for modernization or Westernization. In particular, the Westernization of Turkey rests on three crucial historical turns: firstly, a series of continuous military defeats caused Turks to aggressively modernization as a way to militarily and technologically compete with other Western nations; secondly, the early designers of Turkish secular state relied heavily on French understandings and approaches. And thirdly, the reliance of Turkish political and educational elites on Western epistemologies and expertise thrusted Turkey onto a path of Westernization and Modernity. 

Westernization refers to the establishment of a system based on science and technology in the life of a society where the principles of freedom and equality are adopted as the basis of human rights. This process also provides scientific solutions for the problems encountered in both individual and social life (Ergün, 1990). Westernization basically encourages developing countries to learn and then use what the West has found in science, technology, human rights, prosperity, and art (Başgöz, 2005). This section demonstrates how Turkey's Westernization efforts, which then have effected its education system. 

The first efforts of Westernization in Turkey started during Ottoman State at the end of 18th century (Karpat, Durukan, & Durukan 2002). At that time, Europe still was not at a stage of widely using the scientific applications for steam or mines. However, by the 19th century, Europe had substantial advancements in several areas including education. Such improvements made Turkish authorities believe that Europe was modern and that Turkey needed to do what was possible to reach to the same level of technology and education (Çetinkaya, 2002). The Westernization of Turkey aimed to make political changes in the individual life and social institutions in a democratic direction, improve industrialization for the economy and use science as a reference for higher order of thinking (Koçer, 1983). In efforts of creating a modern Turkish society, many Turkish political and educational elites had their trainings specifically from France during the Ottomans era. The French culture and language were considered as one of the modern languages of the time (Mignolo, 2009). The French culture and the use of their language effected Turkish state and its educational leaders about where to go in terms of obtaining their educational training during that time.

Title: The Effects of Westernization Efforts on the Turkish Education System
Snippet: As for another Westernization effort especially European educators were invited. Educators and experts brought in from the West due to various topics have become another dynamic force that influenced Westernization in Turkish education system. They taught almost in all of the institutions in higher education including military schools of Turkey (Kaplan, 1999). They were first brought from France, and then educators from other European countries and the United States joined them. Some of them worked as teachers, some only provided reports on educational praxis (Turan, 2000). Turkish education system was easily adapted to Western teaching methodologies as there a heavy presence of the experts and educators from the West in Turkish schools during that time. 

The oldest report provided to Ottomans by French experts in terms of Westernization was the one provided by French officer named De Rocheford. He wrote reports about the establishment of a foreign army unit in the Ottoman army in 1716. In 1732, some reports about printing press were also provided by French experts (Zürcher & Gönen, 1999). Claude Alexandre Comte de Bonneval, who actually served in Ottoman army, brought in more French officers to serve after 1730s. In addition, after 1781, Baron de Tott, who came to Istanbul with French ambassador, did substantial work in naval academy. In 1798, at the request of Selim III, German officers joined the army's modernization with the arrival of Officer Von Goetze. In 19th century, Kari Ambrosso Bernard and Sigmund Spitzer, who were from Austria, were the instructors in Turkish medical schools. During the World War I, about 19 faculty members under the chairmanship of Franz Schmidt came to Turkey to teach at Istanbul University (Darülfünun) (Koçer, 1983). 

In terms of Westernization efforts in Turkish education system, obtaining reports from foreign experts and educators continued a fashion of continuous trend even during the Republican era (After 1923) (Kaplan, 1999). Title: Questioning Administration Processes and Autonomy of Higher Education System in Turkey
Snippet: Higher education policies have always been on the agenda of decision makers and politicians in Turkey. Almost every government has changed some certain bodies and structural organizations as well as employment policies at higher education institutions in Turkey. Regarding all changes in the university bodies, it is possible to claim that the history of Turkish universities is also a history of vicious educational reforms as well as "history of exportations". Until 2016, for example, there occurred five mass exportations or dismisses in 1933, 1947, 1960, 1971 and 1983 in Turkish Universities (Mazıcı, 1995). Just before further mass exportations in 2016 and 2017 Turkish government has noted many unusual and radical changes since the early 2000s. For instance, rectorate elections are always referred to as political decisions by ruling governments and presidents and cause many allegations among public and mass media. The election system was partially representation of faculty members before the government removed system of presidency elections held for universities in November, 2016 by means of a decree law no.676 after military coup attempt in July, 2016. Despite the fact that it was a questionable step in terms of representation of faculty members and autonomy of academia, none of the university senates could publish a message questioning the decision. Even before the military coup attempt in July, 2016, the government took several controversial decisions for universities. Autonomy of academia and academic freedoms remained standstill and even seriously fell back. It went seriously worse just after academics for peace petition and signature campaign in January 2016. Many of the signatory academics were criticized harshly by the government and exported from their positions through decree laws just after the military coup attempt in July 2016. On the other hand political campaign, titled "a university for each province" and started in 2006-2007, has advocated inevitable increase in the number of universities and rising demand for many academic personnel to run education processes at the university bodies. The campaign resulted in building up many new universities even in far rural areas of Turkey. Question of quality of education, employment policies, infrastructure and over-education have emerged as more serious educational, social, cultural and financial problems. This paper discusses changes in higher education policies in Turkey from the late Ottoman rule to recent processes. The current study is a descriptive analysis of qualitative and quantitative data based on literature review and text analysis of the newspaper articles and statistical analysis of the data released by Council of Higher Education.

Modernization gains from westernizing and democratizing education

- Quantitative expansion and inclusion of more students into a meritocratic system: democratizing admissions (1968) and subsequent expansion increased the number of middle and high schools, embedding Turkey into pan‑European modernization trajectories and producing a larger technically trained workforce; these expansions coincided with modernization of health and social policy linked to education (e.g., health-behavior improvements associated with more schooling) <cite id="ca96e7c8-2">Democratizing high-school admissions in 1968 coincided with a surge in school numbers and enrollment, laying the groundwork for modernization</cite> <cite id="ca96e7c8-2">The increase became steeper after the 1970s</cite> <cite id="ca96e7c8-2">We examine numbers of primary, middle and high schools over time; after 1968-69, there was a nearly 100% increase in the number of middle schools</cite> <cite id="ca96e7c8-2">The effect of education on health behaviors and obesity in Turkey estimates show cumulative returns to schooling over decades, consistent with modernization and improved policy uptake in the second half of the 20th century</cite>.

Title: The veil as an object of right-wing populist politics: a comparative perspective of Turkey, Sweden, and France
Snippet: In Turkey, until the last decade, the Islamic headscarf was a highly polarising controversy, epitomising the country's religious/secular divide. The republic's founding elites considered the secularisation process identical to modernisation and Westernisation (Berkes 1998). Women's public unveiling was considered a symbol of their emancipation and Turkey's entry into the civilised world (Çınar 2008;Saktanber and Çorbacıoğlu 2008). Especially after the 1970s, due to mass rural-to-urban migration and the rise of Islamist politics, the public use of headscarves became a controversial and polarising topic. In the Turkish case, the headscarf ban at universities, first introduced in 1982, constituted the controversy's focus. However, the ban was not implemented on most campuses until the 28 February 1997 military memorandum, signed by the National Security Council dominated by the military bureaucracy. After the memorandum which aimed at preventing the rise of 'Islamist reactionism', and resulted with the collapse of the coalition government led by between Islamist Welfare Party. Many headscarfed university students dropped out of university. 'Convincing rooms' were set up in some universities, where university staff talked with students to persuade them to take off their headscarves. Two incidents further contributed to the intensification of the headscarf controversy: 1) the prevention of the first headscarfed member of parliament, Merve Kavakçı, from taking her oath in the Turkish parliament in 1999; and 2) in 2007, the controversy about the presidential election of AKP candidate Abdullah Gül for being married to a headscarfed woman, Hayrunnisa Gül.

After the memorandum which aimed at preventing the rise of 'Islamist reactionism', and resulted with the collapse of the coalition government led by between Islamist Welfare Party. Title: Kurdish Linguicide in the "Saddamist" State
Snippet: Many interviewees who attended school in Iraq from the end of the 1970s up to 1990 claim that the repeated shifts between teaching in Kurdish and Arabic was an inten tional strategy to prevent Kurds from reaching fluency in either language. For instance, Faruq Hussein Rashid had to quit school due to the linguistic barriers that were caused by such policy changes, as well as the intimidation, discrimination, and beatings he faced at school. He came from a village to study at a high school in Chamchemal from 1986 to 1989: Besides all the risks, discrimination, torture, and financial pressures we underwent, the time-consuming back and forth travel every day between my village and my school, we also did not understand the language of instruction. Imagine, without having seen or heard the Arabic language before, you are suddenly exposed to the Arabic language and Arabic studying. As you know, Saddam did not provide elec tricity to the villages, so we did not have TV to hear Arabic or even understand city life. I did not understand my teachers, and they did not understand me. There fore, many times students and teachers took advantage of me due to the language barrier. 72 shid experienced the cultural disconnect that often occurs in situations where one language is given supremacy. Learning and mastering a language is strongly connected to understanding a culture: "Children who do not understand the language of instruc tion may be learning a dominant language by submersion but miss out on content learning." 73 Due to the miscommunication and humiliation that resulted from Iraqi language policies many Kurdish students were not able to earn a high enough grade point average in high school for admittance to university. 74 evertheless, despite the Iraqi regime's plan to exclude Kurdish-speaking profes sors from university, or the more wide-ranging effects of the linguicidal policies (such as the erasure of the Kurdish language from public life and the systematic use of lan guage policies to humiliate Kurdish people), Kurds still enrolled in higher education. However, even at the university level they could not acquire the necessary linguistic capital and have adequate access to education.
